newsitem.title: USA: US energy industry split on overseas acreage race.
newsitem.headline: US energy industry split on overseas acreage race.

text.p: Some independent U.S. oil and gas producers are scrambling for overseas acreage often in developing countries, in a bid to hit the next big field, but others question the need.

Flores & Rucks Inc, which today announced it would form a Gulf of Mexico alliance with an energy major to add 500 million barrels of oil equivalent to its reserves, said that giant domestic finds offer lower risk.
"Why should you go anywhere else other than Louisiana," Flores & Rucks chief executive Jim Flores told the Howard Weil energy conference on Wednesday.
That strikes a chord with Pioneer Natural Resources Co, a $3.0 billion indendent formed earlier this week through the merger of MESA Inc and Parker & Parsley Petroleum Co.
Investor Richard Rainwater, who will be the largest single shareholder in Pioneer, warned on Wednesday that the international environment could change very quickly.
"As these countries grow, they may not want to share resources which they need for their own people," he said.

For Seagull Energy Corp the necessity now is to find new ways to grow without the dependence on acquisitions which characterised its past development, chief executive Barry Galt told the conference, and that means going overseas to Egypt, the Ivory Coast and the Russian Republic of Tartarstan.
In 1996, the U.S. accounted for $140 million of the company's $200 million exploration and production spending. This year that will fall to $114 million of a $235 million budget.
"We are not paying $10-$12 million to develop wells in Egypt, it is just a couple of million, this will be a quick paying engine of growth," Galt said.
Apache Corp is also doing its high impact exploration overseas.
"We do our high risk exploration internationally...but we are growing in the U.S. to provide short term cashflow," said Apache chief executive Steven Farris.
Apache has interests in Egypt and the Pacific Rim, especially Western Australia.

Union Pacific Resources Co told Reuters in an interview that it was stepping slowly into the international arena with a venture in Venezuela, but it believed that the U.S. would provide most of its growth.
UPR chief operating officer George Lindahl said that the company had a $1.0 billion capital spending plan this year, most of which is being spent in core areas of the U.S.
"We see years and years of opportunities in the U.S., so it just makes sense to stay here," Lindahl said,"There is a long lead time on international projects, especially in exploration."
Howard Weil analyst John Robertson believes that the difference is one of emphasis.
"They are all chasing the same thing, the opportunity to explore bigger resources which will have a huge impact on reserves," Robertson said.
